notes.meaning: The Lord tells Micah to stand up and present a legal case as if in an open courtroom. God calls on the ancient mountains and hills to listen to what is happening. Because the people have stopped listening to their Lord, the unchanging hills are summoned to serve as silent, faithful witnesses.

Micah addresses the mountains and the deep foundations of the earth, calling them to hear the Lord's charge. God has an indictment—a formal legal case—against His own chosen people. He is ready to lay out the evidence and show that Israel has broken their covenant promises to Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Near Eastern treaties often called on parts of nature, like mountains and hills, to stand as legal witnesses to the pact between a king and his people.

notes.meaning: God tenderly questions His people, asking what wrong He has ever done to make them turn away from Him. He asks if His commands were too heavy a burden, or if He has worn them out with harsh demands. He invites them to bring any fair complaint they have against Him into the open.

Instead of burdening Israel, the Lord reminds them of His great rescue when He freed them from slavery in Egypt. He also gave them gifted leaders, sending Moses to teach His law, Aaron to serve as priest, and Miriam to guide the women. Their whole history began with God's patient kindness and unearned mercy.

The Lord tells His people to recall how King Balak tried to hire the pagan prophet Balaam to curse them, but God made Balaam bless them instead. He also reminds them of their journey from Shittim across the Jordan River to Gilgal, leading into the Promised Land. Remembering these saving deeds proves that the Lord has always stayed faithful and true to His promises.

The speaker wonders what kind of sacrifice could ever satisfy the Lord and make up for sin. The list climbs from standard yearling calves to thousands of rams, vast rivers of olive oil, and finally offering one's own firstborn child. These questions show that no amount of outward ritual or extreme human effort can buy God's favor or clear away guilt.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read these verses as an ancient record of the Moabite king Balak asking Balaam what sacrifices could appease Israel's God, leading into Balaam's answer in verse eight.

notes.meaning: God makes it plain that His true expectations have never been a secret. He does not ask for empty ceremonies, but for people to treat others fairly, to delight in showing mercy, and to walk in humble daily fellowship with Him. Genuine faith shows itself in loving acts toward neighbors and a modest heart before God.

The Lord's voice rings out like a loud warning to the city of Jerusalem. Wise people pay close attention to His name and take His words to heart. The people are told to heed the rod—the painful discipline God is sending—and to recognize the One who ordered it.

The Lord confronts the dishonest business practices filling the city's homes and shops. Merchants were hoarding stolen wealth, using small grain baskets to shortchange buyers, and keeping rigged weights in their bags. God declares that He will never treat as innocent anyone who robs their neighbors with crooked scales.

The wealthy citizens of Jerusalem used violence and intimidation to take advantage of the weak and helpless. Dishonesty had infected the whole community, so that people spoke lies without second thought. Their deceitful words and cruel greed proved how far they had wandered from God's commands.

Because the people refuse to turn from their crimes, God announces that His judgment will strike them down. He will bring severe blows that leave them sick, ruined, and broken by their own wrongdoing. Their stubborn disobedience left them with no shield against His righteous discipline.

The Lord warns them of a frustrating curse where they will labor constantly but never enjoy the fruit of their work. They will eat without feeling satisfied, try to hide valuables that will only end up taken by enemy swords, and plant fields that foreign invaders will harvest. Pressing olives will produce no soothing oil for their bodies, and stomping grapes will yield no wine to drink.

Instead of following God's law, the people copied the wicked customs of King Omri and his son Ahab, who had dragged northern Israel into terrible idol worship. Because Judah chose to walk in those same shameful footsteps, the Lord will turn their city into a ruined wasteland and an object of mockery. Setting aside God's word to follow ungodly rulers always ends in destruction and public disgrace.
